sentences.text: US President Donald Trump is making what appears to be his first foreign visit since his party
got an absolute trouncing
in the US midterm elections, but it's not to a country that hosts one of his golf courses
or to a Persian Gulf oil ally or even to a top 10 world economy. It's
actually
to the Philippines.
That's because there's a massive gathering of leaders from Southeast Asian countries. These relatively small nations
banded together decades ago,
but are starting to play a larger role in an increasingly
AI-driven
world economy,
and they're attracting billions of dollars of investment
to this industry.
But can the ASEAN countries,
as they're known, stick together for mutual benefits?
And how can they play nice with a
with the US
while also keeping the world's second largest economy and massive regional player
China
on side?
Welcome to The Dip, the podcast
for money,
power, and consequences.
I'm Cassandra.
And to delve into this topic, we're going to be zooming over to examine two countries who have
a lot to gain but potentially
a lot to lose. Up first,
I want to say hello to Richard Heydarian
in Manila. He's a political economist
and author of the forthcoming book 50 Shades of Hedging: Trump, China, and Southeast Asia's Struggle for
Autonomy.
Richard, thanks for joining us.
>> My pleasure.
>> And also on the line, we have James Chai joining us from London today. He was
previously a policy advisor to the Malaysian Minister of Economy,
where he worked on flagship policies related to AI innovation, startups, and chips.
He's currently a visiting fellow at the ISEAS.
James, thanks for making the time.
>> Thank you so much for having me.
>> Now, James, you've said before that you're super curious to understand how underdogs
survive and thrive against much more powerful forces.
You've even written about underdogs.
What geoeconomic
underdogs are you keeping an eye on right now?
>> So the one that I think stands out most are Southeast Asian countries.
The reason for that is because the most of the countries there, like you've mentioned, are
very small in size in terms of not only
the economy, but also their global influence.
This necessarily means that they always have to rely on others.
In the past, it was a very
open and free trade economy, which they tried to hold on to.
But at the same time, it is also to work with superpowers.
So Southeast Asia has been
always a theater of
great power conflict,
and this has been a feature
of how Southeast Asia operates and learning how to navigate
big powers and trying to still benefit
from conflict and rivalry
is a feature of Southeast Asia.
>> Now Richard, you're a busy guy. You're on the go today. So viewers,
forgive us for some of the noise you might hear in the background,
but you're such a busy guy when you're not writing a book, hosting a podcast, or
appearing or writing for other news outlets. You also trained, from what I understand,
in martial arts. And I'm wondering,
are there lessons from the gym that can be applied to the world right now?
>> Well, I mean,
I started in Taekwondo
and then I went to boxing and I'm trying to dabble in martial arts, mixed martial
arts right now. And and and I draw that into my understanding of geopolitics.
I mean,
you know, if you you have the right techniques, for instance, in Jiu-Jitsu,
you can take take care of someone who's much larger than you. And I think geopolitical
Jiu-Jitsu should be the name of the game as far as Southeast Asian countries are concerned.

biggest in the world. But if you look at countries like Indonesia, it's already a G20
economy,
one of the largest democracy and Muslim majority nations in the world. If you look at Singapore,
it's already a part of G20 and punches well above its weight. The Vietnamese are already knocking
on the door. And as far as Thailand and the Philippines is concerned, these are not insignificant
economies. And collectively, if you look at the ASEAN, it's the fourth or fifth largest
economic block.
Um so as far as strategic agency is concerned, I want to look at Southeast Asian
countries as helpless
as some of the analysts try to put it. Having said that, of course, they're also
in an important position because in many ways they can
mediate between the superpowers.

uh involving Nvidia, it shows for instance the important role of Southeast Asian particular Singapore
as a part as a potential conduit, right? For the movement of semiconductors
and other important materials. If you look at critical minerals for instance, Indonesia and the Philippines
are among major
producers of nickel.

the table is the PAC SILICA initiative.

of a China-free
supply chain for critical minerals for for semiconductors
and every source of input that is important in terms of shaping the future of global
order. So in that sense, I'm slightly more optimistic in terms of at least in theory
the kind of strategic agency

we have the leadership
and the decisiveness,
of course, that's up up for a question.
>> Yeah, you've teased a lot of the things that I want to get into today with both yourself

big meeting of regional and world leaders?

17th

major issue of course is the South China Sea disputes

ways to de-escalate tensions on that front. And of course, when it comes to critical

cooperation framework is about to be signed

cooperation

whom might not be familiar with the ASEAN countries
and how this organization works together. Why have they banded together to form this ASEAN A

uh
working group? I I I guess you'll know the better term than me. And what do

block uh by five founding members.

uh it is ideologically
uh not on the side of the communists. Uh but through the years,
what it has actually evolved to was to
uh find common ground from very very different
uh political systems,
different economic outlook
uh into something that they could agree on.
Uh there is a huge
um
achievement
track record in terms of like signing a lot of trade deals,

having
uh a secretariat,

uh US, China,
and uh the major powers.

uh way of operating whereby
individual countries, no matter how different they are,
member states do not interfere with
each other's political affairs.

as an institutionalized
way like the EU,
where they have like common
sort of legislative
bodies, common executive bodies.
Largely ASEAN has been criticized
as being not as effective
in terms of getting a lot of key issues
forward.
The only thing that they have really made a lot of achievements on
is maintaining
relative peace relative to other parts of the world as well as a lot of like
free trade agreements that really
increase the
trade profile as well as foreign direct investments that matter to all of the Southeast Asian
member states.

containing

vision,

also very closely to this ASEAN summit is the APEC summit that

What this necessarily means is that this summit
has not been
probably thought about
significantly
in terms of like what they want to achieve compared to

more
issues relating to tariff,
um
reciprocal trade. All of those are like very very big items.

a relative acceptance

uh in a lot of the tariff discussions

Trump
um walking away from it. So I don't see a major major deliverable
that
is very important to the US, but
that appearance

the Koreans, the Europeans to get involved in that.

what the Philippines wants to do with Pax Silica is to move up there. And of

TSMC,
some Japanese and Korean companies, not to mention Americans
looking at the Philippines
as a way to diversify
away from Taiwan,
also as a way to create new nodes for semiconductor
critical
minerals processing
hubs.

ambigu- ambiguous about this or a bit iffy about this is that Trump is on on his
last leg and the Philippines Marcos administration
is also entering its last leg. So 2020 countries could have new presidents with new directions.

covered
multiple US administration throughout decades
and each of them comes up with a big initiative, Trans-Pacific Partnership with Obama,

with with with Biden and now Pak Silica.

James, Malaysia

it is a part of ASEAN.

What's it like to get an industry like this off the ground or to further develop
it so that it is a a major regional, if not global, player?
>> So
that's a really good question because ultimately,
I think it comes with a combination
of the natural
conditions
that a country has, as well as whether that country could take advantage of it quick enough.
I think the example of data centers in Malaysia is worth highlighting because
the state of Johor, which is where most of the hotspot is,
went from a country with less than 10 MW
just 3 years ago
to now 1,000
MW at the minimum. And people are really looking at a multiple
a few multiples of that.
It started off from having the natural conditions
of competitive
costs when comes to land, water, electricity,
as well as construction costs.
It comes from having a high density of subsea cables around that part of
Southeast Asia, which really opened up all of these opportunities.
And the country really took a very adaptive approach in terms of like responding to these
billion dollar investments
by branded names,
AWS,
Microsoft, as well as the
the Chinese side of
Huawei, Alibaba, and so on.
So I I think it took a combination of all of that. And then
through a very iterative approach, determining
a lot of the AI strategy
going forward. What is interesting is that all Southeast Asian countries actually had
their own AI
or similar
strategy before
ChatGPT was released in 2022.
And they changed all of their AI strategies
after that
as did many parts of the world. And suddenly things that have worked well in their favor,
like AI infrastructure
relating to data centers, became front and center.
So to some extent, it came from an external
wave of what
the superpowers wanted,
but it also came with some degree of agency on their part in determining where
they would like to play the most, where they think that they have the highest opportunity of
winning.
And and that
became a really defining fact
in terms of how they look at AI.
>> Richard,
I can't help but wonder. It seems like the last year has been a really defining

When we step back and look at chips and the semiconductor
business,

important strategic asset?

you know, Malaysia has a very affordable energy infrastructure.

not only, you know, semiconductor
industry, but they want also to be part of the artificial intelligence
game in the coming years or so. The Thailand, the Thai also developed their own initiative here.
I mean,
the sense I'm getting here is that, you know, um
there's
there's a fear that maybe we're talking about a bubble and that bubble might burst earlier

national security and geopolitical consideration.

the profit margins or the cost curves are showing, but this is precisely because

our base of, I mean, data centers or or the basic infrastructure for our frontier research

in media res, right? We're in the middle of things being built, right? The pyramids are
